summary:
Adamawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across every state of the federation, including to visitors and tourists: entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, and 10 years for anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of one, or who supports the registration and operation of gay clubs, societies and organisations. Same-sex sexual acts between men are separately criminalised under the secular Criminal Code with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Sharia criminal law is the layer that varies by state. The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note and Wikipedia's survey of the statute both identify twelve northern states where sharia penal codes apply to Muslims, with death as the maximum penalty for men: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Adamawa is not named in either list, so the sources do not support a death-penalty finding for Adamawa. The federal 14-year framework and the nationwide arrest climate nonetheless apply here in full.

Enforcement against LGBTQ+ people is documented as routine. NGOs record tens of LGBT+ arrests per year in Nigeria, and the same country-policy note reports that police and Islamic police subject LGBT+ people to beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. Sharia courts have imposed at least four death sentences since 2022, none carried out. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice, updated in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under sharia provisions in some northern states.

Trans people face lethal violence and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged. Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement: in March 2025 a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. Kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), who pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and completed on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
A 2022 federal court ruled sections of the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act unconstitutional and unenforceable. The sources do not record any consequent change in policing practice, and the FCDO's August 2026 advice continues to warn of arrest and imprisonment under the same statute.

Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians lived in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public. Whether any such proposal has been enacted is not settled by the sources available here, and no Adamawa-specific provision is recorded.

Adamawa's position relative to the sharia states is the main point of divergence from the wider northern pattern: the twelve states carrying the death penalty for men under sharia zina provisions do not include Adamawa in the lists supplied, while the federal SSMPA and Criminal Code exposure is identical to every other state.

Bobrisky's imprisonment arose from currency-abuse charges rather than from her gender expression, but the case is the clearest evidence in these sources of how a trans detainee's housing between male and female sections is decided by prison authorities rather than by rule.
localsOnly:
Residents of Adamawa live under the same criminal statutes as visitors: the SSMPA's 14-year maximum for entering a same-sex marriage or civil union, the 10-year penalty for assisting or witnessing one or for supporting gay organisations, and up to 14 years for same-sex acts between men under the Criminal Code.

NGOs document tens of LGBT+ arrests per year across Nigeria, with beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture reported at the hands of police. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text, and extortion through demanded bribes is a documented feature of stops by police.

Nigeria provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no legal mechanism for recognition of a same-sex partnership, marriage or spouse. Trans people have no statutory protection against being housed in a prison section corresponding to their birth sex, and press treatment of the Bobrisky case indicates that placement is left to the discretion of the Nigerian Correctional Service.

Sharia penal codes apply to Muslims in the twelve northern states named in the sources, which do not include Adamawa; residents therefore face the federal secular framework rather than sharia zina provisions on the evidence available.
